slides.title: Fasting plasma glucose
slides.eyebrow: Carbohydrate metabolism · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Plasma  ·  Units: mg/dL, mmol/L  ·  Population: Not pregnant
What it is used for: Screening for prediabetes and diabetes, finding the cause of symptoms of high or low glucose, and monitoring side effects of some long-term medicines that affect glucose.

slides.title: Fasting plasma glucose
slides.eyebrow: Carbohydrate metabolism · Reference values and decision limits

rows: People who are not pregnant, after fasting for at least 8 hours
People who are not pregnant (WHO/IDF criteria)
People who are not pregnant, after fasting for at least 8 hours

slides.title: Fasting plasma glucose
slides.eyebrow: Carbohydrate metabolism · Reference values and decision limits · 1/2
rows: People who are not pregnant, after fasting for at least 8 hours
People who are not pregnant (WHO/IDF criteria) — WHO: 6.1–6.9 mmol/L; 2-hour glucose, if measured, < 7.8 mmol/L. The ADA/NIDDK lower limit is 100 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L).

slides.title: Fasting plasma glucose
slides.eyebrow: Carbohydrate metabolism · Reference values and decision limits · 2/2
rows: People who are not pregnant, after fasting for at least 8 hours — Diagnosis usually requires a repeat test. Pregnancy uses different criteria.

slides.title: Fasting plasma glucose
cols: Prediabetes and diabetes are the most common causes. Other possible causes include an overactive thyroid gland (hyperthyroidism), pancreatic problems including pancreatitis, stress from surgery, very serious illness or trauma, adrenal gland problems and certain medicines.
With diabetes: some diabetes medicines and other glucose-lowering medicines, not eating enough (especially after taking diabetes medicine) and more physical activity than usual.

slides.title: Fasting plasma glucose
cols: Without diabetes, low glucose is uncommon; possible causes include liver or kidney disease, underactive adrenal glands, some pituitary disorders, an underactive thyroid gland (hypothyroidism), malnutrition, certain medicines and alcohol use disorder.

slides.title: Fasting plasma glucose
bullets: Limitations: What a result means depends on which test was done, other test results and the medical history.

slides.title: Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c)
slides.eyebrow: Carbohydrate metabolism · What it is used for · 1/3
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood  ·  Units: %

What it is used for: Used to screen for or diagnose type 2 diabetes and prediabetes, and to monitor glucose control in people who already have diabetes or prediabetes. It is not used to diagnose type 1 diabetes, although it may be used for monitoring.

slides.title: Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c)
slides.eyebrow: Carbohydrate metabolism · What it is used for · 2/3
bullets: Physiology: Blood glucose attaches to hemoglobin in red blood cells: the higher the glucose, the more hemoglobin becomes glucose-coated. The glucose stays attached for the life of the red cell (about three months), so A1C reflects average glucose over the past 2–3 months.

slides.title: Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c)
slides.eyebrow: Carbohydrate metabolism · What it is used for · 3/3
bullets: A1C is a weighted average: glucose levels in the preceding 30 days contribute more to the result than those 90–120 days earlier. Clinically significant changes in glucose therefore show up in A1C without waiting 120 days for red-cell turnover.

slides.title: Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c)
slides.eyebrow: Carbohydrate metabolism · Reference values and decision limits

slides.title: Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c)
slides.eyebrow: Carbohydrate metabolism · Reference values and decision limits
rows: People who are not pregnant — IFCC: 39–47 mmol/mol (ADA, Table 2.2). Pregnancy uses different cutoffs for some tests.
People who are not pregnant — 6.5% or above (IFCC: ≥ 48 mmol/mol; ADA, Table 2.1). Diagnosis is usually confirmed with a second test. Pregnancy uses different cutoffs for some tests.

slides.title: Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c)
bullets: High: A high A1C is a sign of high blood glucose from diabetes. Because more than one test is often used for diagnosis, a raised result is usually followed by a repeat A1C or a different test, most often a fasting blood glucose test or an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT).

slides.title: Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c)
bullets: Pre-analytics: No fasting is needed: the person can eat and drink before the test, and blood can be drawn at any time of day.
Interferences: Certain medicines, such as opioids and some HIV medicines, may affect the result, so all medicines taken should be reported. Pregnancy may also affect the result.

slides.title: Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c)
bullets: Conditions that change red-cell life span—recent blood loss, sickle cell disease, erythropoietin treatment, hemodialysis or transfusion—can change A1C. Very low iron (iron-deficiency anemia) can give a falsely high A1C, and kidney failure or liver disease can also cause false results.

slides.title: Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c)
bullets: Common hemoglobinopathies (e.g., HbS, HbC, HbE, HbSC, elevated HbF) can falsely raise or lower A1C, depending on the variant and the assay method. NIDDK advises against using A1C in patients with HbSS, HbCC or HbSC.

Suspect a hemoglobinopathy when A1C is unexpected or at odds with other diabetes tests, is below 4% or above 15%, differs from self-monitored glucose, or changes markedly after the laboratory changes its A1C method.

slides.title: Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c)
bullets: Limitations: A1C should not be used to diagnose type 1 diabetes, gestational diabetes or cystic fibrosis–related diabetes.

slides.title: Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c)
bullets: For diagnosis, a venous sample goes to a laboratory using an NGSP-certified method. Point-of-care A1C may be used for diagnosis only with devices approved for diagnosis (FDA) in certified (CLIA) laboratories performing moderate- or higher-complexity testing, by trained staff (ADA 2.2b); other point-of-care results are not used for diagnosis.

slides.title: Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c)
bullets: A1C and blood glucose tests do not always agree: a glucose test may show diabetes when A1C does not, and vice versa. For this reason, tests are repeated before a diagnosis is made.

A1C does not show sudden, temporary rises or falls in glucose. Re-measuring the same sample can give a slightly different result; NIDDK’s example is that 6.8% on one test could read 6.4–7.2% on a repeat.

slides.title: Oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT)
slides.eyebrow: Carbohydrate metabolism · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood: fasting and after the glucose drink  ·  Units: mg/dL

What it is used for: The OGTT helps detect type 2 diabetes, prediabetes and gestational diabetes. It is used to diagnose gestational diabetes; outside pregnancy it is sometimes used to confirm prediabetes or type 2 diabetes.
The test shows how well the body processes sugar. In pregnancy it may follow a non-fasting 1-hour glucose challenge (screening) test whose result is too high; NIDDK gives 135 to 140 mg/dL or higher.

slides.title: Oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT)
slides.eyebrow: Carbohydrate metabolism · Reference values and decision limits

slides.title: Oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT)
slides.eyebrow: Carbohydrate metabolism · Reference values and decision limits
rows: People who are not pregnant — Value 2 hours after glucose intake. Pregnancy uses different cutoffs.
People who are not pregnant — 200 mg/dL or above, 2 hours after glucose intake. Diagnosis is usually confirmed with a second test; pregnancy uses different cutoffs.

slides.title: Oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT)
bullets: High: A high glucose level on the OGTT may indicate diabetes. In pregnancy, glucose that is high two or more times during the test may indicate gestational diabetes.

High: For blood glucose tests in general, prediabetes and diabetes are the most common causes of high glucose. Other possible causes include an overactive thyroid (hyperthyroidism), pancreatic problems including pancreatitis, stress from surgery, very serious illness or trauma, adrenal problems (Cushing’s syndrome, pheochromocytoma) and certain medicines.

slides.title: Oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT)
bullets: Pre-analytics: Fasting for at least 8 hours is required before the test.
A fasting blood sample is taken, the person drinks a liquid high in sugar, and another blood sample is taken 2 hours later. In pregnancy, blood is drawn several times over 2 to 3 hours.

slides.title: Oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT)
bullets: Interferences: Glucose naturally rises and falls with eating and exercise, and sickness and stress can also affect results. Small differences in temperature, equipment or sample handling affect fasting and OGTT glucose measurements more than A1C.

slides.title: Oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT)
bullets: Limitations: The OGTT is more expensive and harder to give than fasting plasma glucose or the glucose challenge test. A diagnosis is usually confirmed with a second test.

slides.title: Fructosamine
slides.eyebrow: Carbohydrate metabolism · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Blood

What it is used for: According to NIDDK, fructosamine (or glycated albumin) may be considered as another measure of average glucose in patients with hemoglobinopathies when an accurate A1C cannot be obtained—for example in HbSS, HbCC or HbSC, where A1C should not be used.
Physiology: The fructosamine test measures glucose molecules linked to protein molecules in the blood. The assay is also called glycated serum protein.

slides.title: Fructosamine
bullets: Limitations: Fructosamine reflects a much shorter period than A1C—usually about 2–3 weeks, versus the preceding 3 months for A1C—so the two tests describe different time windows.

NIDDK patient information gives fructosamine as an example of alternative tests that scientists are working on for people with hemoglobin variants; it shows average glucose over about 3 weeks. Whether it is an option is for the doctor to decide.

slides.title: Insulin
slides.eyebrow: Hormones · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Blood from a vein

What it is used for: An insulin test is used with other tests to find the cause of hypoglycemia (the main reason), evaluate how much insulin the pancreas is making, help diagnose an insulinoma (a benign insulin-making tumor) or see whether it has come back after surgery, and monitor pancreatic islet cell transplantation in type 1 diabetes. It is often combined with C-peptide, fasting blood glucose and A1C tests.

slides.title: Insulin
slides.eyebrow: Hormones · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: Insulin is made by the pancreas and helps glucose move from the blood into cells, where it is used for energy. Normally insulin and blood glucose rise and fall together: after eating, glucose rises and the pancreas releases more insulin; as glucose falls, it releases less.

Too much insulin can make blood glucose too low (hypoglycemia). With too little insulin, or if the body doesn't respond well to it, glucose builds up in the blood (hyperglycemia), which over time can lead to type 2 diabetes. In insulin resistance the pancreas makes more insulin to keep glucose in a healthy range, but over time it may not keep up, leading to prediabetes and type 2 diabetes.

slides.title: Insulin
cols: If insulin is high and glucose is normal or a little high, the body may be making extra insulin because cells aren't responding normally (insulin resistance).
If insulin is low and glucose is high, the pancreas may not be making enough insulin — possible causes include type 1 diabetes and pancreatitis.

slides.title: Insulin
cols: If insulin is high or normal and glucose is low, there may be hypoglycemia from too much insulin — possible causes include an insulinoma, Cushing's syndrome or taking more insulin than needed; C-peptide or proinsulin tests may help find the cause.

slides.title: Insulin
bullets: Pre-analytics: Fasting for 8 to 12 hours is usually needed. Biotin (vitamin B7) supplements, or supplements that include biotin, should be stopped for at least a day before the test.

Interferences: Some people who take insulin develop antibodies against it, which can interfere with insulin tests and cause inaccurate results — the provider should know about any insulin medicine. Also, some insulin tests measure certain types of insulin medicine differently.

slides.title: Insulin
bullets: According to FDA, biotin technology is used in many laboratory tests, including hormone tests. In people who take more biotin (vitamin B7) than the recommended daily intake — it is found in multivitamins, prenatal vitamins and hair, skin and nail supplements — results can be falsely high or falsely low, depending on the test principle.

Limitations: An insulin test is not usually used to diagnose diabetes — diabetes is diagnosed with blood glucose tests. Because insulin varies with glucose, one result is usually not enough by itself and other tests are needed; reference ranges vary between laboratories.

slides.title: Insulin
bullets: According to NIDDK, health care professionals may not test for insulin resistance: the test for it is primarily used only in research studies, while prediabetes is diagnosed with blood glucose tests (A1C, fasting plasma glucose, sometimes an OGTT).

Labs often use different methods and therefore different reference ranges, so a result is compared with the range on your own lab report, not with ranges found elsewhere. Results from different labs can't be compared with each other, and trends are best followed in the same lab.

slides.title: C-peptide
slides.eyebrow: Hormones · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Blood (sometimes 24-hour urine)

What it is used for: C-peptide helps find the cause of hypoglycemia (whether it is linked to high insulin), manage diabetes treatment — even in people who take insulin — monitor treatment of an insulinoma, and tell type 1 from type 2 diabetes when the diagnosis is uncertain.

Physiology: C-peptide is a chain of amino acids the pancreas makes while making insulin. It enters the blood at the same time and in equal amounts as insulin but stays in the blood longer, and it is unaffected by outside sources of insulin such as diabetes medicines. So C-peptide gives an accurate picture of how much insulin the body is making naturally.

slides.title: C-peptide
cols: High C-peptide usually means the body is making too much insulin: type 2 diabetes, Cushing's syndrome, an insulinoma, kidney failure, or low blood potassium. After treatment for an insulinoma, a fall in C-peptide means treatment is working; a rise may mean the tumor is back.

Low C-peptide may mean the body isn't making enough insulin: type 1 and, in some cases, type 2 diabetes, taking too much insulin for diabetes (which may block the pancreas from making its own), a severe infection, Addison disease or liver disease.

slides.title: C-peptide
bullets: Pre-analytics: Usually blood is tested, sometimes all urine collected over 24 hours. For a blood test, fasting for 8–12 hours may be needed; sometimes C-peptide is also tested after eating to see levels while the pancreas is actively working.

slides.title: C-peptide
bullets: Limitations: C-peptide is not used to diagnose diabetes — blood and urine glucose tests are used for that. The meaning of the result depends on age, health, medicines taken and other tests such as blood glucose.

slides.title: C-peptide
bullets: Labs often use different methods and therefore different reference ranges, so a result is compared with the range on your own lab report, not with ranges found elsewhere. Results from different labs can't be compared with each other, and trends are best followed in the same lab.

slides.title: Type 2 diabetes
bullets: Screening, diagnosis and monitoring. Anyone with diabetes symptoms is tested; without symptoms, people with risk factors are tested (for example age 35 or older, overweight or obesity plus another risk factor, or past gestational diabetes). A diagnosis is usually confirmed with a second test.

slides.title: Type 2 diabetes
rows: Reflects average blood glucose over about 3 months; no fasting is needed.
Taken after at least 8 hours without food, usually in the morning.

slides.title: Type 2 diabetes
rows: After fasting for at least 8 hours a sugary drink is taken and blood is drawn 2 hours later. It is more expensive and less convenient than the other tests.
Taken at any time — when there are diabetes symptoms and waiting for a fasting test is not wanted.

slides.title: Type 2 diabetes
rows: With diabetes, A1C at least twice a year; more often if treatment goals are not being met.
Diabetic kidney disease often has no symptoms: urine albumin is checked yearly (in type 2 diabetes; in type 1 after 5 years).
Blood test showing how well the kidneys filter blood; yearly with diabetes.

slides.title: Type 2 diabetes
rows: With type 2 diabetes the risk of heart problems is higher, so the lipid panel may be checked more often.

slides.title: Type 2 diabetes
rows: A1C ≥ 6.5% (≥ 48 mmol/mol), or fasting glucose ≥ 126 mg/dL (≈7.0 mmol/L), or 2-hour OGTT ≥ 200 mg/dL (≈11.1 mmol/L)
Diabetes is likely. It is usually confirmed with a second test.
A1C 5.7–6.4% (39–47 mmol/mol), or fasting glucose 100–125 mg/dL (≈5.6–6.9 mmol/L; WHO: 110–125 mg/dL, 6.1–6.9 mmol/L), or OGTT 140–199 mg/dL (≈7.8–11.0 mmol/L)
Prediabetes is likely (ADA criteria; WHO defines impaired fasting glycaemia by glucose only, from 6.1 mmol/L); yearly testing for type 2 diabetes is recommended.
Random glucose ≥ 200 mg/dL (≈11.1 mmol/L) + diabetes symptoms
Diabetes is likely. This cut-off is used only together with symptoms.

slides.title: Type 2 diabetes
rows: Changes in red cells or hemoglobin (for example a hemoglobin variant) may have affected the result — the clinician may repeat testing or choose another test.

slides.title: Type 2 diabetes
bullets: A1C can be unreliable with blood loss, transfusion, iron-deficiency anemia, kidney failure, liver disease and hemoglobin variants. It is not used to diagnose type 1 or gestational diabetes.
mmol/L values are converted from the source’s mg/dL cut-offs (approximate). Home glucose meters cannot be used to diagnose diabetes.

slides.title: Gestational diabetes
bullets: Diabetes that occurs only during pregnancy. All pregnant women without known diabetes are tested at 24–28 weeks; type 2 diabetes is also tested for at the first prenatal visit (within 15 weeks).

slides.title: Gestational diabetes
rows: No fasting needed: blood is drawn 1 hour after a sweet glucose drink.
To confirm the diagnosis if screening shows high glucose. In pregnancy, blood is drawn every hour for 2–3 hours.
Testing for type 2 diabetes at the first prenatal visit or within the first 15 weeks (especially with risk factors).

slides.title: Gestational diabetes
rows: After gestational diabetes, testing for type 2 diabetes is recommended — usually within 12 weeks after delivery.

slides.title: Gestational diabetes
rows: Glucose challenge (1 hour) ≈135–140 mg/dL (≈7.5–7.8 mmol/L) or higher
Positive screen — a fasting OGTT may be needed.
Two or more high values on the OGTT

slides.title: Gestational diabetes
bullets: A1C is not used to diagnose gestational diabetes. mmol/L values are converted from the source’s mg/dL (approximate).

slides.title: Metabolic syndrome
bullets: You may have metabolic syndrome if you have three or more of the listed conditions. Waist size, blood pressure and blood tests (fasting glucose, cholesterol, triglycerides) are assessed.

slides.title: Metabolic syndrome
rows: Blood glucose after fasting for 8–12 hours.
One criterion is consistently high triglycerides.
One criterion is low HDL cholesterol.

slides.title: Metabolic syndrome
rows: One metabolic syndrome criterion (harmonized cut point ≥ 150 mg/dL; the NHLBI page says “consistently more than 150”).
HDL < 40 mg/dL (≈1.0 mmol/L) in men or < 50 mg/dL (≈1.3 mmol/L) in women
Fasting glucose ≥ 100 mg/dL (≈5.6 mmol/L) or taking glucose-lowering medicine
One criterion — high blood sugar: 100–125 mg/dL (≈5.6–6.9 mmol/L) means high blood sugar or prediabetes; ≥ 126 mg/dL (≈7.0 mmol/L) may mean diabetes.

slides.title: Metabolic syndrome
rows: Waist > 40 inches in men / > 35 inches in women; blood pressure consistently ≥ 130/85
Non-lab criteria; waist thresholds may vary by race and ethnicity.

slides.title: Metabolic syndrome
bullets: For children the clinician sets the measures and cut-offs. mmol/L values are converted from the source’s units (approximate).

slides.title: Reference values and decision limits

slides.title: A patient with sickle cell anemia (HbSS) needs an assessment of average glucose. What does NIDDK advise?
options: Use A1C as usual — hemoglobin variants do not affect it, so no alternative test such as fructosamine is needed.
Do not use A1C; consider alternatives such as glycated serum protein (fructosamine) or glycated albumin.
Repeat A1C after an overnight fast to remove the interference, then interpret it as usual.
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: NIDDK advises against A1C in HbSS, HbCC and HbSC and suggests considering alternative tests.

Basis: NIDDK professional page: do not use A1C in HbSS, HbCC or HbSC; consider glycated serum protein or glycated albumin.

slides.title: A nonpregnant person without symptoms has an A1C in the diabetes range. What should happen before a diagnosis is made?
options: Nothing more — a single A1C in the diabetes range is enough.
Confirm the result right away with a point-of-care A1C device at the bedside.
Repeat testing on a different day with A1C or another diabetes test.
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: without symptoms, the diagnosis is confirmed by a repeat test on a different day.

Basis: NIDDK: without symptoms, an A1C showing diabetes or prediabetes should be confirmed by a repeat test on a different day; ADA: point-of-care A1C may be used for diagnosis only on a device approved for diagnosis in a certified laboratory (2.2b).

slides.title: What preparation is required before a diagnostic OGTT?
options: No preparation — it can be done right after a meal.
Fasting is needed only in pregnancy.
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: the OGTT requires fasting for at least 8 hours.

Basis: NIDDK: fast at least 8 hours before an OGTT; the glucose challenge test needs no fasting.

slides.title: In a nonpregnant person, which OGTT measurement do the NIDDK cutoffs of 7.8–11.0 mmol/L (140–199 mg/dL) for prediabetes and 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) or above for diabetes apply to?
options: The fasting sample taken before the drink.
The sample taken 2 hours after glucose intake.
The sample 1 hour after a non-fasting glucose drink.
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: the OGTT column in the table refers to the value 2 hours after glucose intake.

Basis: NIDDK table: OGTT values are measured 2 hours after glucose intake; the table applies when not pregnant.

slides.title: Over roughly what period does fructosamine reflect average blood glucose?
options: Only glucose at the moment of sampling
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: NIDDK states fructosamine usually reflects about 2–3 weeks of average glucose.

Basis: NIDDK: fructosamine and glycated albumin reflect a much shorter period than A1C, usually about 2–3 weeks.

slides.title: In which situation do NIDDK professional materials suggest considering fructosamine?
options: In pregnant patients, as the standard test used to diagnose gestational diabetes.
In all patients, as a routine replacement for A1C in diabetes management.
In patients with hemoglobinopathies when an accurate A1C cannot be obtained.
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: this is the situation in which NIDDK suggests considering fructosamine or glycated albumin.

Basis: NIDDK: when an accurate A1C cannot be obtained in a hemoglobinopathy, fructosamine or glycated albumin may be considered; gestational diabetes is checked with the glucose challenge test or OGTT.

slides.title: Neuroendocrine regulation of carbohydrate metabolism. Type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus?
bullets: 1. Glucose homeostasis: insulin (β cells) is the only glucose-lowering hormone: it enhances glucose entry into tissues, glycogenesis, lipogenesis, and inhibits gluconeogenesis and lipolysis; counter-regulatory hormones – glucagon, adrenaline, cortisol, growth hormone, thyroid hormones.
2. Nervous system: sympathetic activity (adrenaline) enhances glycogenolysis and glucagon secretion; incretins (GLP-1, GIP) increase insulin secretion after a meal.

slides.title: Neuroendocrine regulation of carbohydrate metabolism. Type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus?
bullets: 3. Type 1 DM – autoimmune destruction of β cells, absolute insulin deficiency; markers: autoantibodies (GAD65, IA-2, insulin, ZnT8), low C-peptide; tendency to ketoacidosis.
4. Type 2 DM – insulin resistance and relative insulin secretion deficiency; associated with obesity and metabolic syndrome; C-peptide initially normal/high.
5. Other types: gestational DM, monogenic (MODY), diseases of the exocrine pancreas, drug- or endocrinopathy-related.

slides.title: Neuroendocrine regulation of carbohydrate metabolism. Type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus?
bullets: 6. Diagnostic criteria are the same for both types: fasting plasma glucose ≥7.0 mmol/L, 75 g OGTT 2-hour value ≥11.1, HbA1c ≥6.5%, or random ≥11.1 mmol/L with symptoms.

slides.title: Modern laboratory diagnosis of diabetes mellitus?
bullets: 1. Diabetes criteria (ADA/WHO, venous plasma): fasting glucose ≥7.0 mmol/L (≥126 mg/dL; fasting ≥8 hours), 2-hour glucose at 75 g OGTT ≥11.1 mmol/L, HbA1c ≥6.5% (48 mmol/mol; NGSP-certified method standardized to DCCT), or random glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L with symptoms of hyperglycemia.
2. For a diagnosis without unequivocal hyperglycemia, two abnormal results are needed (two tests from one sample or on two different days).
3. Prediabetes (ADA): fasting 5.6–6.9 mmol/L (impaired fasting glucose), OGTT 2-hour 7.8–11.0 (impaired glucose tolerance), HbA1c 5.7–6.4%.

slides.title: Modern laboratory diagnosis of diabetes mellitus?
bullets: 4. Conditions in which HbA1c is unreliable: sickle cell and other hemoglobinopathies (method-dependent), second–third trimester of pregnancy, hemodialysis, recent blood loss/transfusion, erythropoietin therapy, G6PD deficiency, HIV – in these only plasma glucose is used.

5. Preanalytics: because of glycolysis, glucose at room temperature falls by ~5–7% per hour – centrifuge the sample immediately or use a tube with a glycolysis inhibitor; a glucometer result is not for diagnosis.

slides.title: Modern laboratory diagnosis of diabetes mellitus?
bullets: 6. Determining type and complications: autoantibodies, C-peptide; ketones; urine albumin/creatinine ratio, eGFR, lipids; in pregnancy at 24–28 weeks a 75 g OGTT (92/180/153 mg/dL ≈ 5.1/10.0/8.5 mmol/L).

slides.title: Laboratory diagnosis of complications of diabetes mellitus?
bullets: 1. Acute complications: diabetic ketoacidosis (glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L or a history of diabetes, β-hydroxybutyrate ≥3.0 mmol/L, pH <7.30 and/or HCO3 <18 mmol/L – 2024 consensus), hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state (glucose >33.3 mmol/L [>600 mg/dL], effective osmolality >320, without significant ketoacidosis), hypoglycemia (level 2 <3.0 mmol/L).

2. Diabetic nephropathy (kidney disease): urine albumin/creatinine ratio – A2 3–30 mg/mmol, A3 >30 mg/mmol (confirmed in 2 of 2–3 samples within 3 months), eGFR (creatinine, CKD-EPI) – at least once a year.

slides.title: Laboratory diagnosis of complications of diabetes mellitus?
bullets: 3. Glycemic control: HbA1c (usually every 3–6 months), home/continuous glucose monitoring; fructosamine – when HbA1c is unreliable.
4. Risk of macroangiopathy: lipid profile (total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, triglycerides, non-HDL cholesterol).
5. Others: urinalysis (glucosuria, ketonuria, proteinuria, infection), electrolytes (potassium in DKA), B12 level in those taking metformin.
